title: How wide to quote
objectives: Set the width of a quote from your uncertainty.

screens.title: How sure is a range?
screens.prose: The interviewer asks: on the sum of two dice, give me a range around 7 you are two-thirds sure of. Slide the half-width and watch how much of the chance the range holds.
screens.question: What is the narrowest range centred on 7 that holds at least two thirds of the chance?

options.why: You stopped at 6 to 8, which holds 16/36, under one half. Widen it by one each side.
That holds 30/36, more than needed. A narrower range already passes two thirds.
That holds everything. It is safe and says nothing about where the total will land.

hints.text: Watch the shaded probability as the half-width grows.
At half-width 2 the shaded share is 24/36.
Half-width 2 gives 5 to 9, which holds $24/36 = 2/3$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the smallest half-width whose shaded share reaches 0.6667.

explain.text: Half-width 1 holds 16/36 and half-width 2 holds 24/36, exactly two thirds. So 5 to 9 is the narrowest range that passes. The gain per step shrinks, because the outer totals are rare.

screens.title: Count the rolls
screens.prose: The **width** of a range is its high end minus its low end. The range 6 to 8 has width 2. The shaded cells are the rolls it holds.
screens.question: What share of the 36 rolls does 6 to 8 hold? Give a fraction or four decimal places.

hints.text: Count the shaded cells.
Totals 6, 7 and 8 have 5, 6 and 5 rolls.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the shaded cells and divide by 36.

byKey.totals-equal: You treated the 11 totals as equally likely: 3/11. Totals near 7 have more rolls.
byKey.totals: You counted 3 totals out of 36 rolls. Count the rolls, 16 of them.

explain.text: Totals 6, 7 and 8 have 5, 6 and 5 rolls: 16 of the 36. So 6 to 8 holds $16/36 = 4/9$. A range of width 2 holds less than half the chance.

screens.title: Wider
screens.prose: Widen the range to 4 to 10, width 6.
screens.question: What share of the rolls does 4 to 10 hold?

hints.text: It may be quicker to count the rolls outside.
Outside are totals 2, 3, 11 and 12: 1, 2, 2 and 1 rolls.
$36 - 6 = 30$ rolls inside.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the six rolls outside and subtract from 36.

byKey.totals-equal: You treated the 11 totals as equally likely: 7/11. Count rolls, not totals.

explain.text: Only six rolls fall outside: totals 2, 3, 11 and 12. So 4 to 10 holds $30/36 = 5/6$. Tripling the width from 2 to 6 took the share from 4/9 to 5/6.

screens.title: A width limit
screens.prose: Many interviewers set a rule: "your width may be at most 2." So your range spans three totals, such as 6 to 8.
screens.question: Which range of width 2 holds the most rolls?

options.why: You moved the range off centre. 5 to 7 holds 15 rolls against 16 for 6 to 8.
You moved the range off centre. 7 to 9 holds 15 rolls against 16 for 6 to 8.
That range has width 4. The rule allows at most 2.

hints.text: The middle totals have the most rolls.
Total 7 has 6 rolls, 6 and 8 have 5 each.
Centre on 7: 6 to 8 holds 16 rolls, the most for width 2.

feedback.correct: 6 to 8: the centre holds the most.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the width at 2 and centre it where the rolls are densest.

explain.text: Under the width limit, centring on 7 holds 16 rolls. Shifting one step either way holds 15. This total is symmetric, so its fair value is also where the chance is densest, and the range sits there.

screens.title: Quote under the limit
screens.prose: Now the sum of three dice, fair value 10.5. Your range doubles as a **quote**: you buy at the low end and sell at the high end. The width may be at most 2.
screens.question: Set the two ends: width at most 2, centred on the fair value.

hints.text: Start from the fair value and step out the same distance each way.
Width 2 means 1 each side of 10.5.
Low end 9.5, high end 11.5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the width at most 2 and the middle at 10.5.

byKey.crossed: Your low end is above your high end. You would buy higher than you sell.
byKey.zero: You gave zero width on an uncertain total. Any trade at that price is a coin flip with no edge.
byKey.too-wide: Your width is more than 2. The interviewer’s rule caps it at 2.
byKey.off-centre: Your range is not centred on 10.5. The middle of your quote should be your fair value.

explain.text: A width of 2 centred on 10.5 gives 9.5 to 11.5. It holds the totals 10 and 11, a quarter of the rolls. Under a tight limit, the centre matters more than the width.

screens.title: The trade-off
screens.prose: A toy game on two dice. You quote $7 \pm h$. Half the time the interviewer knows the total and trades only when it is outside your quote. Otherwise an uninformed trader pays you $h$, with chance $1 - h/4$. Drag the dot along the profit curve.
screens.question: Where does the profit per game peak?

options.text: At zero width, where most trades happen.
options.why: At zero width the informed interviewer picks you off on almost every roll. The profit there is about −£0.97.

options.text: In between, near a half-width of 2.5 to 3.

options.why: At half-width 5 nobody trades with you at all. You earn nothing and lose nothing.

hints.text: Drag the dot along the curve and watch the caption.
At $h = 1$ the profit is negative; at $h = 2.5$ it is about £0.27.
The peak is near $h = 2.7$: between the two extremes.

feedback.correct: In between: about £0.28 a game near $h = 2.7$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the profit curve at a few half-widths.

explain.text: A tight quote trades a lot but the informed interviewer picks it off. A wide quote is safe but nobody trades. The best width sits in between, here near a half-width of 2.7.

screens.title: A tight market
screens.prose: The interviewer rolls one die and says: make me a tight market on it, width at most 1.
screens.question: Which quote answers the question?

options.why: You quoted the full range. It can never be wrong, so it says nothing, and its width is 5.
You gave zero width on a die you cannot see. Every roll lands away from 3.5, so you have no edge either way.
You centred on 4.5. The fair value of a die is 3.5.

hints.text: Tight means narrow, but not zero.
Centre on 3.5 and use the width you are allowed.
3 to 4: width 1, centred on 3.5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the width allowed, centred on the fair value.

byKey.full: You quoted the full range. It can never be wrong, so it says nothing.
byKey.zero: You gave zero width on an uncertain roll. Width follows uncertainty, and a die has plenty.

explain.text: A tight market uses the width allowed, centred on the fair value: 3 to 4. The full range ignores the question, and zero width ignores the uncertainty. Interviewers test both mistakes.

screens.title: Both sides trade
screens.prose: Back to three dice, quoting 9.5 to 11.5. The interviewer sells you one at 9.5. Later another trader buys one from you at 11.5. Mark each trade at the fair value, 10.5.
screens.question: What is your total P&L after both trades, in pounds?

widget.accept: £2: £1 on each trade, the full width.
widget.label: P&L in pounds

hints.text: Each trade earns its distance from fair value.
The sale at 11.50 is £1 above fair value.
$+1 + 1 = 2$: the full width.

feedback.correct: £2: the full width of the quote.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add what each trade earns against fair value.

byKey.half: That is one trade. The sale adds another £1.
byKey.zero: Your position is flat, but you bought low and sold high. That locks in the width.

explain.text: Buying at 9.50 and selling at 11.50 locks in £2, whatever the dice show. Each single trade earns half the width against fair value. That is why width is the market maker’s pay.

screens.title: Width from uncertainty
screens.prose: You traded coverage against width. For a near-normal total, a quote of $\mu \pm k\sigma$ holds a share fixed by $k$. $$P(|X - \mu| \le \sigma) \approx 0.68.$$ On two dice, $7 \pm 2.42$ holds the totals 5 to 9, which is 2/3.
screens.question: A contract always pays £6. How wide should your quote be, in pounds?

widget.accept: 0: the payout is known, so there is no uncertainty to cover.
widget.label: Width in pounds

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The payout is certain: how much uncertainty is there to cover?

byKey.one: You kept a habit width. With $\sigma = 0$ there is nothing to cover.
byKey.two: You kept a habit width. With $\sigma = 0$ there is nothing to cover.

explain.text: A known payout has $\sigma = 0$, so $\mu \pm k\sigma$ has zero width for any $k$. Quote 6 at 6, or say it is known. Width is a measure of doubt.

screens.title: A formula for coverage
screens.prose: On two dice, the totals above $7 + k$ have $1 + 2 + \dots + (5 - k)$ rolls, which is $\tfrac{(5-k)(6-k)}{2}$. The same number sit below $7 - k$.
screens.question: Write the share of the 36 rolls inside $7 - k$ to $7 + k$.

hints.text: Count the rolls outside on both sides, then subtract from 36.
Outside: $2 \times \tfrac{(5-k)(6-k)}{2} = (5-k)(6-k)$ rolls.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take both tails away from the whole.

byKey.one-side: You took away only one tail. Rolls below $7 - k$ are outside too.
byKey.outside: That is the share outside the range. Subtract it from 1.

explain.text: Both tails hold $(5-k)(6-k)$ rolls together, so the inside share is $1 - (6-k)(5-k)/36$. It gives 4/9, 2/3 and 5/6 for $k = 1, 2, 3$, as you counted. At $k = 5$ it is 1: the whole range.

screens.title: Coverage in code
screens.prose: Check any range on any number of dice by listing every roll. Return a `Fraction`, so 4/9 stays 4/9.
screens.question: Complete `coverage(lo, hi, n_dice)`.

    total lies in [lo, hi], ends included."""
    ...
widget.solution:
from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import product


def coverage(lo, hi, n_dice):
    """Exact share of rolls of n_dice dice whose
    total lies in [lo, hi], ends included."""
    rolls = list(product(range(1, 7), repeat=n_dice))
    inside = sum(lo <= sum(r) <= hi for r in rolls)
    return Fraction(inside, len(rolls))
widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests. Each result must be a Fraction equal to the exact share.

hints.text: `product(range(1, 7), repeat=n_dice)` lists every roll.
Count the rolls with `lo <= sum(r) <= hi`.
Return `Fraction(inside, len(rolls))`.

feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Include both ends, and return a Fraction.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that the `...` is replaced.

explain.text:
Listing all $6^n$ rolls makes the share exact. Both ends count, so `coverage(7, 7, 2)` is 1/6. On three dice, 8 to 13 holds 73/108, the first symmetric range past one half.

screens.title: Before results
screens.prose: A share trades at £20. Its daily moves have an sd of 1%, or 20p, and you quote fair value ±20p. Tomorrow the company reports results. The options market prices an sd of 3% for that day.

state.caption: Your calm-day quote, ±20p, holds far less on results day

screens.question: To hold the same share of moves, what half-width should you quote, in pounds?

widget.accept: £0.60: three times the sd, so three times the half-width.
widget.label: Half-width in pounds

hints.text: Your half-width was one sd.
The sd triples from 20p to 60p.
Keep the half-width at one sd: 3% of £20 = £0.60.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the half-width at one sd, and the sd is now 3% of £20.

byKey.same: You kept the calm-day width. Results day moves three times as far, so you would be picked off.
byKey.variance: You scaled by the variance, nine times. Width scales with the sd, three times.

explain.text: Width follows the sd. Results day triples it, so the quote goes from ±20p to ±60p and holds the same share of moves. Real quotes in a share are far tighter than one day’s sd, but they too widen when volatility rises.

ideas: A range of fair value ± k sd holds a share set by k. On two dice, 5 to 9 holds 2/3.
Tight quotes trade more and earn the width more often; wide quotes lose less when someone knows more.
Width follows uncertainty: zero for a known payout, wider when the sd rises, as before results.

formula.name: Coverage of a quote
formula.note: For a near-normal total. Two dice: $1 - (6-k)(5-k)/36$ exactly.

summary.trap: Quoting the full range when asked for a tight market, or zero width on a quantity you cannot see.
